title: Armenia notes - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Cowen's travel notes on Armenia praise its intellectual and cultural life and describe deep, largely accepted Russian influence over energy, trade and security, warm relations with Iran, and acute fear of Turkey; he dismisses claims Armenia will become the next Poland.

insights.claim: Russia is embedded in virtually every Armenian institution: it supplies most of Armenia's energy, is its number one trading partner, and Russian troops protect Armenia from Turkey.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Armenia's economy and security remain structurally tied to Russia, limiting Western pivot scenarios.
insights.quote: Russia supplies most of their energy, and is the number one trading partner.  Russian troops protect them from Turkey.

insights.claim: Armenians' main discontent with Russia is that Putin did not protect them more in the war with Azerbaijan, not a view that Russia is evil.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Public sentiment does not support a decisive break from Russia.

insights.claim: Russians do not need a passport to enter and live in Armenia, and most immigrants are Russian.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Facilitates Russian capital and labor flows into Armenia.
insights.quote: A Russian does not even need a passport to enter and live in Armenia.

insights.claim: Armenia has close relations with Iran and regards it as a partial counterweight to both Turkey and Russia.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Armenia is a potential conduit for Iran ties, relevant to sanctions and regional alignment.
insights.quote: They regard the country as a partial counterweight to Turkey, and for that matter Russia.
insights.locator: Armenia has close relations with Iran

insights.claim: Armenians are highly conscious of the existential risk posed by Turkey and are deeply preoccupied with their history and maps.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Persistent security fears shape Armenian policy choices.
insights.quote: People in Armenia are very conscious of the x-risk represented by Turkey.
insights.locator: Armenia has close relations with Iran

insights.claim: Mount Ararat, a national symbol on Armenian currency, is in Turkey and very likely to remain so.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.quote: yet it is now part of Turkey and is very likely to remain so

insights.claim: Cowen rejects the take that Armenia will be the next Poland.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Tempers bullish convergence narratives for Armenian growth.
insights.quote: no it will not be the next Poland
insights.locator: Here is someone else’s exaggerated take

insights.claim: Armenia, with just over three million people, remains intellectual, has won the chess Olympiad gold three times in recent memory, and arguably alone preserves the strengths of the former Soviet Union.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Human-capital base is notable relative to population.
insights.quote: It feels more like the former Soviet Union than Russia does.

insights.claim: Armenia is not dirt cheap but much cheaper than most of Europe, and most tourists at monasteries are Russians and Iranians rather than Westerners.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Tourism is regionally sourced, with untapped Western demand.

insights.claim: Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia are currently near-perfect travel destinations—comfortable, exotic, not overtouristed—and will never get better to visit.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Signals rising tourism flows to the South Caucasus.
insights.quote: They will never get better to visit, and right now they are pretty close to perfect as destinations.
insights.locator: I would put it this way
